claim: The γ-tubulin ring complex (γTuRC) is a 2.2 MDa complex that forms an asymmetric ring of γ-tubulin subunits.
source: γTuRC is a large, 2.2 MDa complex that forms an asymmetric ring of γ-tubulin subunits (Zheng et al., 1995; Moritz et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Zheng et al., 1995; Moritz et al., 1998).

claim: The γ-tubulin ring is thought to act as an initial template for the microtubule.
source: This ring is thought to act as an initial template for the MT (Moritz et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Moritz et al., 2000).

claim: In vitro studies with purified human and Xenopus γTuRCs have shown that these can catalyze the nucleation of new microtubules.
source: In vitro studies with purified human and Xenopus γTuRCs have shown that these can indeed catalyze the nucleation of new MTs (Choi et al., 2010; Thawani et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Choi et al., 2010; Thawani et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020).

claim: γTuRC acts with the MT polymerase, XMAP215/ch-TOG, to nucleate microtubules.
source: Recent studies have also shown that γTuRC acts with the MT polymerase, XMAP215/ch-TOG, to nucleate MTs (Thawani et al., 2018; Flor-Parra et al., 2018; Gunzelmann et al., 2018; King et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Thawani et al., 2018; Flor-Parra et al., 2018; Gunzelmann et al., 2018; King et al., 2020a).

claim: Structural studies of γTuRCs from yeast, frogs (Xenopus laevis), and humans revealed remarkable conservation of the γ-tubulin ring structure.
source: Structural studies of γTuRCs from yeast, frogs (Xenopus laevis), and humans revealed remarkable conservation of the γ-tubulin ring structure, although the composition of γTuRC differs substantially across these organisms (Kollman et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b; Consolati et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Kollman et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b; Consolati et al., 2020).

claim: The composition of γTuRC differs substantially across yeast, frogs, and humans.
source: Structural studies of γTuRCs from yeast, frogs (Xenopus laevis), and humans revealed remarkable conservation of the γ-tubulin ring structure, although the composition of γTuRC differs substantially across these organisms (Kollman et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b; Consolati et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Kollman et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b; Consolati et al., 2020).

claim: The pitch and diameter of the γ-tubulin ring appears to be incompatible with that of the assembled MT lattice.
source: Intriguingly, the pitch and diameter of the γ-tubulin ring appears to be incompatible with that of the assembled MT lattice.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Thawani et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020) in the following sentence.

claim: γTuRC undergoes a conformational change to reduce its diameter before it can nucleate microtubules.
source: This suggests that γTuRC undergoes a conformational change to reduce its diameter before it can nucleate MTs (Thawani et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Thawani et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020) and is presented as a suggestion based on structural observations.

claim: Cdk5rap2 recruits γTuRC to the centrosome and Golgi.
source: The centrosomal scaffold protein Cdk5rap2, which recruits γTuRC to the centrosome and Golgi (Andersen et al., 2003; Bond et al., 2005; Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010; Mennella et al., 2012; Lawo et al., 2012), has been shown to increase γTuRC's nucleation activity (Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010; Roubin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Andersen et al., 2003; Bond et al., 2005; Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010; Mennella et al., 2012; Lawo et al., 2012).

claim: Cdk5rap2 has been shown to increase γTuRC's nucleation activity.
source: The centrosomal scaffold protein Cdk5rap2, which recruits γTuRC to the centrosome and Golgi (Andersen et al., 2003; Bond et al., 2005; Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010; Mennella et al., 2012; Lawo et al., 2012), has been shown to increase γTuRC's nucleation activity (Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010; Roubin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010; Roubin et al., 2013).

claim: The γ-tubulin nucleation activator (γTuNA or CM1) sequence in Cdk5rap2's N-terminus is critical to bind and activate γTuRC.
source: Previous domain-mapping studies found that the γ-tubulin nucleation activator (γTuNA or CM1) sequence in Cdk5rap2's N-terminus is critical to bind and activate γTuRC (Figure 1A; Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010).

claim: The γTuNA sequence is well-conserved across yeast, nematodes, flies, frogs, and humans.
source: The γTuNA sequence is well-conserved across yeast, nematodes, flies, frogs, and humans (Samejima et al., 2010; Conduit et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2017; Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010), and identical γTuNA domains have been identified in related centrosomal and Golgi proteins such as myomegalin (Roubin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Samejima et al., 2010; Conduit et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2017; Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010).

claim: Identical γTuNA domains have been identified in related centrosomal and Golgi proteins such as myomegalin.
source: The γTuNA sequence is well-conserved across yeast, nematodes, flies, frogs, and humans (Samejima et al., 2010; Conduit et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2017; Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010), and identical γTuNA domains have been identified in related centrosomal and Golgi proteins such as myomegalin (Roubin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Roubin et al., 2013).

claim: A bipartite version of γTuNA is present in the microtubule branching factor, TPX2.
source: A bipartite version of γTuNA is also present in the microtubule branching factor, TPX2 (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; King and Petry, 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; King and Petry, 2020b).

claim: Previously, γTuNA had little effect on the activity of antibody-purified Xenopus γTuRC in vitro.
source: Previously we reported that γTuNA had little effect on the activity of antibody-purified Xenopus γTuRC (Thawani et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work by the authors (Thawani et al., 2020).

claim: Liu et al. (2020) observed that γTuNA had minimal effect on antibody-purified Xenopus γTuRC activity in vitro.
source: Our observation was seemingly corroborated by independent in vitro and structural data published that same year (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Liu et al., 2020).

claim: Addition of wildtype γTuNA triggered an increase in MT nucleation of up to ~75-fold in Xenopus egg extract.
source: In contrast, addition of wildtype γTuNA triggered an increase in MT nucleation of up to ~75-fold in a titration series (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification of MT nucleation in extract with γTuNA titration.

claim: The Xenopus F71A mutant equivalent to the human F75A mutant did not significantly increase MT number even at the highest concentration (3.6 µM).
source: The Xenopus F71A mutant equivalent to the human F75A mutant (Figure 1B), hereafter referred to as 'F75A', did not significantly increase MT number even at the highest concentration (3.6 µM, Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing no significant increase in MT nucleation with F75A mutant.

claim: The γTuNA domain activates MT nucleation in extract and requires the F75 residue.
source: Thus, the γTuNA domain activates MT nucleation in extract and requires the F75 residue, validating prior studies (Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 1C-D) and citations to prior published work (Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010).

claim: The γTuNA domain has no effect on γTuRC assembly.
source: Using sucrose gradients to fractionate mock and γTuNA-treated extracts, we also conclude that the γTuNA domain has no effect on γTuRC assembly, ruling out one possible explanation for this increase in MT number (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, which displays sucrose gradient profiles showing no shift in γTuRC distribution with γTuNA treatment.

claim: Full-length Cdk5RAP2 is unlikely to affect γTuRC assembly.
source: While we cannot rule out that full-length Cdk5RAP2 might affect γTuRC assembly, we believe this is also unlikely as recent work has demonstrated that γTuRC can be assembled via heterologous expression of just γTuRC components and the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 AAA ATPase complex, without addition of a CM1-containing protein (Zimmermann et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Zimmermann et al., 2020) and represents an inference based on that work.

claim: A single round of depletion removed >75% of γ-tubulin signal indicating a depletion of γTuRC.
source: With a single round of depletion, we observed a loss of >75% of γ-tubulin signal indicating a depletion of γTuRC (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E, which displays a Western blot showing loss of γ-tubulin signal after pulldown with γTuNA-coupled beads.

claim: Exogenous γTuNA no longer activated MT nucleation in γTuRC-depleted extracts.
source: By contrast, exogenous γTuNA no longer activated MT nucleation in γTuRC-depleted extracts (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F, which displays TIRF microscopy images showing no MT nucleation activation by γTuNA in γTuRC-depleted extract.

claim: The γTuNA domain requires the universal MT template, γTuRC, to activate MT nucleation.
source: Hence, the γTuNA domain requires the universal MT template, γTuRC, to activate MT nucleation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 1F) showing loss of γTuNA activation effect in γTuRC-depleted extract.

claim: Wildtype γTuNA-coated beads formed large MT asters mimicking the potent MT nucleation of the centrosome.
source: We found that wildtype γTuNA-coated beads formed large MT asters mimicking the potent MT nucleation of the centrosome (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, which displays oblique TIRF images of MT asters from wildtype γTuNA beads.

claim: The F75A mutant beads formed severely impaired asters.
source: In contrast, the F75A mutant beads formed severely impaired asters (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, which displays oblique TIRF images showing impaired MT aster formation from F75A mutant beads.

claim: Wildtype γTuNA beads attached and formed large MT asters in vitro, indicating that these beads had retained γTuRC and any other necessary MT nucleation factors.
source: Critically, we observed that wildtype γTuNA beads attached and formed large MT asters in vitro, indicating that these beads had retained γTuRC and any other necessary MT nucleation factors (Figure 2C, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Video 1, which displays time-lapse TIRF imaging of MT aster growth from wildtype γTuNA beads.

claim: γTuNA domains are sufficient to specify new sites of γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation.
source: From this we conclude that γTuNA domains are sufficient to specify new sites of γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 2B-C) showing MT aster formation from γTuNA-coated beads.

claim: The ability of F75A beads to weakly nucleate asters is due to residual, but persistent, binding of γTuRC.
source: Finally, the ability of F75A beads to weakly nucleate asters points to residual, but persistent, binding of γTuRC. We believe this is due to the low stringency wash particular to this experiment, as we do not detect γTuRC on F75A beads after higher stringency washes in subsequent experiments (western blots in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Figure 3D-E, which display Western blots showing no γTuRC binding to F75A beads after higher stringency washes.

claim: γTuRC is the dominant co-precipitant for wildtype versions of human and Xenopus γTuNA.
source: Our mass spectrometry analysis revealed that γTuRC is the dominant co-precipitant for wildtype versions of human and Xenopus γTuNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, which displays volcano plots and a table of proteins enriched by wildtype γTuNA baits.

claim: Wildtype γTuNA is a dimer.
source: Our SEC data revealed that wildtype γTuNA is a dimer (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C, which displays size-exclusion chromatography traces and peak retention volumes indicating dimer formation.

claim: γTuNA dimerization is dependent on residues I67, L70, and L77.
source: By comparing the SEC traces for the double, triple, or quadruple mutants from both Xenopus and human γTuNAs, we found that γTuNA dimerization was dependent on residues I67, L70, and L77 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, which displays size-exclusion chromatography traces showing loss of dimerization with mutations at these residues.

claim: The double hydrophilic mutants (I67D/L70D) from both human and Xenopus versions were entirely monomeric.
source: The double hydrophilic mutants (I67D/L70D) from both human and Xenopus versions were entirely monomeric.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 3B) showing SEC traces indicating monomer formation for I67D/L70D mutants.

claim: Mutating residues F63 or F75 to alanine had no deleterious effect on γTuNA dimerization.
source: We compared the SEC traces for these point mutants and found that mutating residues F63 or F75 to alanine had no deleterious effect on γTuNA dimerization (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, which displays size-exclusion chromatography traces showing maintained dimerization with F63A or F75A mutations.

claim: Individually mutating residues I67, L70, or L77 increasingly interfered with dimerization, resulting in intermediate populations between full dimer and full monomer.
source: By contrast, individually mutating residues I67, L70, or L77 increasingly interfered with dimerization, resulting in intermediate populations between full dimer and full monomer (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C, which displays size-exclusion chromatography traces showing intermediate peaks for I67A, L70A, and L77A mutants.

claim: Mutation of the L70 or L77 residues resulted in the most drastic impairment of dimerization.
source: Mutation of the L70 or L77 residues resulted in the most drastic impairment, further confirming that this central region is crucial for γTuNA dimerization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 3B-C) showing the most significant shifts in SEC peaks for L70A and L77A mutants.

claim: Both human and Xenopus double aspartate mutants (I67D/L70D), as well as the human triple mutant (I67D/L70D/L77D) did not bind γTuRC.
source: We found that both human and Xenopus double aspartate mutants (I67D/L70D), as well as the human triple mutant (I67D/L70D/L77D) did not bind γTuRC, indicating that loss of dimerization results in loss of γTuRC binding (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and F, which displays Western blots showing no γTuRC binding to these mutants.

claim: Loss of dimerization results in loss of γTuRC binding.
source: We found that both human and Xenopus double aspartate mutants (I67D/L70D), as well as the human triple mutant (I67D/L70D/L77D) did not bind γTuRC, indicating that loss of dimerization results in loss of γTuRC binding (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and F, which displays Western blots showing correlation between loss of dimerization and loss of γTuRC binding.

claim: The intermediate dimer mutants (I67A, L70A, or L77A) had correspondingly intermediate levels of γTuRC binding ability.
source: Interestingly, we found that the intermediate dimer mutants (I67A, L70A, or L77A) had correspondingly intermediate levels of γTuRC binding ability (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, which displays Western blots showing varying levels of γTuRC binding for intermediate dimer mutants.

claim: The I67A mutant retained its ability to bind γTuRC.
source: The I67A mutant, for example, was only weakly impaired in terms of dimerization (Figure 3B) and subsequently retained its ability to bind γTuRC (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, E, and G, which displays SEC traces and Western blots showing maintained γTuRC binding for I67A mutant.

claim: As dimerization was increasingly impaired in the L70A and L77A mutants, γTuRC binding became increasingly weaker.
source: As dimerization was increasingly impaired in the L70A and L77A mutants, γTuRC binding became increasingly weaker (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G, which displays quantification of γTuRC binding showing correlation between dimerization impairment and binding ability.

claim: The L77A mutant had complete loss of γTuRC binding.
source: In the most extreme example, the L77A mutant, which had the most substantial dimerization defect, had complete loss of γTuRC binding (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G, which displays quantification showing no γTuRC binding for L77A mutant.

claim: The F75A mutant did not bind γTuRC.
source: Critically, the known F75A mutant did not bind γTuRC, as expected (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-G, which displays Western blots showing no γTuRC binding for F75A mutant.

claim: F75A does not affect γTuNA dimerization.
source: As our SEC data shows that F75A does not affect γTuNA dimerization, we conclude that both γTuNA dimerization and the F75 residue are required for binding γTuRC (Figure 3B and D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, which displays SEC traces showing maintained dimerization for F75A mutant.

claim: Both γTuNA dimerization and the F75 residue are required for binding γTuRC.
source: As our SEC data shows that F75A does not affect γTuNA dimerization, we conclude that both γTuNA dimerization and the F75 residue are required for binding γTuRC (Figure 3B and D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and D-G, which displays SEC traces and Western blots showing that both dimerization and F75 are necessary for γTuRC binding.

claim: Forcing γTuNA dimerization via the addition of a constitutively dimeric coiled-coil domain (GCN4) did not rescue the ability of the intermediate dimer mutants to bind γTuRC.
source: Finally, we found that forcing γTuNA dimerization via the addition of a constitutively dimeric coiled-coil domain (GCN4) did not rescue the ability of the intermediate dimer mutants to bind γTuRC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, which displays SEC traces and Western blots showing no rescue of γTuRC binding with GCN4 fusion.

claim: Simply bringing intermediate dimer mutants within tight proximity is not enough to induce restoration of the proper γTuRC binding interface.
source: This suggests that simply bringing intermediate dimer mutants within tight proximity is not enough to induce restoration of the proper γTuRC binding interface.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing no rescue of γTuRC binding with GCN4 fusion.

claim: Wildtype γTuNA triggered an increase in MT nucleation when compared to the buffer control.
source: As before, wildtype γTuNA triggered an increase in MT nucleation, when compared to the buffer control (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing increased MT nucleation with wildtype γTuNA.

claim: The F75A mutant had little effect on extract MT levels.
source: The F75A mutant had little effect on extract MT levels (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing no significant increase in MT nucleation with F75A mutant.

claim: The L77A mutant did not increase MT nucleation.
source: Similarly, the L77A mutant, which cannot bind γTuRC in extract (Figure 3G), did not increase MT nucleation (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing no increase in MT nucleation with L77A mutant.

claim: The I67A mutant activated MT nucleation to ~50% of wildtype levels.
source: Intriguingly, when we examined the intermediate γTuRC-binding mutants I67A and L70A, we found that the I67A mutant activated MT nucleation to ~50% of wildtype levels, but L70A had no activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, which displays quantification showing I67A mutant activates MT nucleation to ~50% of wildtype levels.

claim: The L70A mutant had no activity in extract.
source: Intriguingly, when we examined the intermediate γTuRC-binding mutants I67A and L70A, we found that the I67A mutant activated MT nucleation to ~50% of wildtype levels, but L70A had no activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, which displays quantification showing L70A mutant has no significant activity.

claim: There is a threshold to γTuRC's activation in extract.
source: However, because the L70A mutant had little activity in extract (~6%, Figure 4B) but retained ~35% binding ability (Figure 3G), it appears that there is a threshold to γTuRC's activation in extract.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 3G, which displays quantification showing divergence between binding ability and activation effect for L70A mutant.

claim: The addition of γTuNA triggered a 5-fold increase in MT mass as compared to the buffer control in vitro.
source: Strikingly, the addition of γTuNA triggered a 5-fold increase in MT mass as compared to the buffer control (Figure 5B, Video 2 and Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, which displays quantification of MT mass over time showing 5-fold increase with γTuNA.

claim: Wildtype γTuNA sharply increased the γTuRC nucleation rate from 1.2 MTs/s to 24.5 MTs/s (~20-fold increase).
source: These quantifications revealed that wildtype γTuNA sharply increased the γTuRC nucleation rate from 1.2 MTs/s to 24.5 MTs/s (~20-fold increase, Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D, which displays quantification of MT number over time and nucleation rates showing ~20-fold increase with γTuNA.

claim: There was a slight increase in mean MT growth speed (+0.2 µm/min) with wildtype γTuNA, but this did not translate into a significant effect on MT length.
source: While there was a slight increase in mean MT growth speed (+0.2 µm/min), this did not translate into a significant effect on MT length (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-F, which displays violin plots of MT growth speeds and lengths showing slight increase in speed but no significant effect on length.

claim: Wildtype γTuNA saturated the assay within 30 s.
source: We also found that wildtype γTuNA saturated our assay within 30 s (Figure 5C), with a decreased nucleation rate of 0.15 MTs/s that remained constant for the remainder of the experiment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, which displays quantification showing saturation of MT nucleation within 30 s.

claim: γTuNA's effect is almost exclusively due to a direct ~20-fold increase in γTuRC activity and not due to altered MT dynamics.
source: Thus, we conclude that γTuNA's effect is almost exclusively due to a direct ~20-fold increase in γTuRC activity and not due to altered MT dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 5) showing increased nucleation rate but minimal effect on MT dynamics.

claim: Bulky N-terminal tags on γTuNA completely ablated its ability to activate γTuRC, instead turning it into a specific γTuRC repressor.
source: Incidentally, we also found that bulky N-terminal tags on γTuNA completely ablated its ability to activate γTuRC, instead turning it into a specific γTuRC repressor (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, which displays TIRF images showing inhibition of MT nucleation with N-terminally tagged γTuNA.

claim: The F75A mutant did not increase MT mass in vitro.
source: As expected, the F75A mutant did not increase MT mass in vitro (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, which displays quantification of MT mass over time showing no increase with F75A mutant.

claim: Both the F75A and L77A mutants had no significant effect on the initial γTuRC nucleation rate.
source: Furthermore, both the F75A and L77A mutants had no significant effect on the initial γTuRC nucleation rate (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, which displays quantification of nucleation rates showing no significant effect for F75A and L77A mutants.

claim: L77A caused a weakly significant increase in MT number beginning at 150 s.
source: However, we did observe that L77A caused a weakly significant increase in MT number beginning at 150 s (Figure 5C, p ~ 0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, which displays quantification of MT number over time showing a late increase with L77A mutant.

claim: Around 150 s L77A increased γTuRC's nucleation rate 1.4-fold when compared to buffer.
source: Similarly, we found that around 150 s L77A increased γTuRC's nucleation rate 1.4-fold when compared to buffer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, which displays quantification of nucleation rate at saturation showing 1.4-fold increase with L77A mutant.

claim: Beyond 150 s, the L77A mutant triggered a delayed increase in MT mass.
source: Beyond 150 s, the L77A mutant triggered a delayed increase in MT mass (Figure 5B), a behavior not observed in extract (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, which displays quantification of MT mass over time showing a late increase with L77A mutant.

claim: The presence of other factors in extract blocks impaired dimer mutants like L77A from interacting with or stimulating γTuRC.
source: From this discrepancy, we inferred that the presence of other factors in extract blocks impaired dimer mutants like L77A from interacting with or stimulating γTuRC.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 4 and Figure 5) showing divergent behavior of L77A mutant in extract versus in vitro.

claim: A simple deterministic model based on the initial nucleation rates was sufficient to capture most of the behavior in the system, except for the L77A mutant of γTuNA.
source: We found that a simple deterministic model based on the initial nucleation rates was sufficient to capture most of the behavior in our system, except for the L77A mutant of γTuNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3, which displays simulated MT mass and number over time matching experimental data except for L77A mutant.

claim: The nucleation rate completely captured the effect of wildtype and F75A γTuNA on MT number and mass.
source: Using a single constant growth speed for all conditions, we found that the nucleation rate completely captured the effect of wildtype and F75A γTuNA on MT number and mass (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3, which displays simulated MT mass and number over time matching experimental data for wildtype and F75A.

claim: For L77A, the simulation suggests a two-phase behavior where its effect on nucleation rate increases at some late stage, possibly due to a shift from an impaired dimer state to complete dimer when bound to γTuRC.
source: For L77A, our simulation suggests a two-phase behavior where its effect on nucleation rate increases at some late stage, possibly due to a shift from an impaired dimer state to complete dimer when bound to γTuRC (Figure 5—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3F, which displays a model for L77A's two-phase behavior.

claim: Wildtype γTuNA's effect on MT nucleation is due to a direct increase in γTuRC activity without altering MT dynamics.
source: Regardless, both the in vitro and simulated data demonstrate that wildtype γTuNA's effect on MT nucleation is due to a direct increase in γTuRC activity without altering MT dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental and simulation data from the current study (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3) showing increased nucleation rate but minimal effect on MT dynamics.

claim: Stathmin negatively regulates MT nucleation by γTuRC.
source: We sought to first confirm that stathmin negatively regulated MT nucleation by γTuRC (as in our previous work; Thawani et al., 2020), and then determine whether γTuNA had any effect on this.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work by the authors (Thawani et al., 2020).

claim: At double and triple the endogenous concentration of stathmin in extract (~3 µM or ~4.2 µM final), there was a drastic loss of MT nucleation and polymerization.
source: At double and triple the endogenous concentration of stathmin in extract (~3 µM or ~4.2 µM final), we observed a drastic loss of MT nucleation and polymerization (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing loss of MT nucleation with high stathmin concentrations.

claim: γTuNA was still able to activate MT nucleation even at the highest concentration of stathmin tested, with a ~ five-fold increase in the number of MTs.
source: Surprisingly, γTuNA was still able to activate MT nucleation (Figure 6A), even at the highest concentration of stathmin tested, with a ~ five-fold increase in the number of MTs (Figure 6B, 2.7 µM stathmin).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing γTuNA activation of MT nucleation even with high stathmin concentrations.

claim: Stathmin resulted in losses of 59% and 81% MT mass at 2.5 or 4 µM stathmin, respectively, in vitro.
source: We next tested γTuRC in the presence of either 2.5 or 4 µM stathmin and found that stathmin resulted in losses of 59% and 81% MT mass, respectively (Figure 6C, 'No γTuNA' conditions).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing loss of MT mass with stathmin.

claim: Addition of γTuNA to stathmin and γTuRC rescued MT mass.
source: Interestingly, addition of γTuNA to stathmin and γTuRC rescued MT mass (Figure 6C–D, '+ γTuNA').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing rescue of MT mass with γTuNA addition.

claim: At 4 µM stathmin with γTuNA, MT mass levels were restored to the level of the γTuRC control (no stathmin, no γTuNA).
source: In fact, at 4 µM stathmin with γTuNA, MT mass levels were restored to the level of the γTuRC control (no stathmin, no γTuNA).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 6C-D) showing restoration of MT mass levels with γTuNA addition.

claim: γTuNA indirectly counteracts the effect of stathmin in extract by increasing the efficiency of γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation at lower tubulin concentrations.
source: This suggested that γTuNA indirectly counteracts the effect of stathmin in extract by increasing the efficiency of γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation at lower tubulin concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 6) showing γTuNA activation of MT nucleation in the presence of stathmin.

claim: At 7 µM tubulin, γTuRC had little detectable activity with only ~1–2 MTs nucleated over a five-minute time course.
source: As expected, at this critical concentration γTuRC had little detectable activity with only ~1–2 MTs nucleated over a five-minute time course (Figure 6E, buffer).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E, which displays TIRF microscopy images showing minimal MT nucleation at 7 µM tubulin.

claim: γTuRC activity increased twenty-five-fold when in the presence of γTuNA at 7 µM tubulin.
source: By contrast, γTuRC activity increased twenty-five-fold when in the presence of γTuNA (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing 25-fold increase in MT nucleation with γTuNA at 7 µM tubulin.

claim: γTuNA decreases γTuRC's critical tubulin concentration.
source: Thus, γTuNA decreases γTuRC's critical tubulin concentration, or restated, increases its ability to nucleate MTs at lower tubulin concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 6E) showing increased γTuRC activity at low tubulin concentrations with γTuNA.

claim: The γTuNA domain is an obligate dimer.
source: We showed that the γTuNA domain is an obligate dimer and that both dimerization and the F75 residue are crucial for binding γTuRC, providing the first biochemical validation for a recent structure of γTuRC bound to a putative γTuNA dimer (Wieczorek et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 3) showing γTuNA dimerization and its requirement for γTuRC binding.

claim: Both dimerization and the F75 residue are crucial for binding γTuRC.
source: We showed that the γTuNA domain is an obligate dimer and that both dimerization and the F75 residue are crucial for binding γTuRC, providing the first biochemical validation for a recent structure of γTuRC bound to a putative γTuNA dimer (Wieczorek et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 3) showing requirement of both dimerization and F75 for γTuRC binding.

claim: This study provides the first biochemical validation for a recent structure of γTuRC bound to a putative γTuNA dimer.
source: We showed that the γTuNA domain is an obligate dimer and that both dimerization and the F75 residue are crucial for binding γTuRC, providing the first biochemical validation for a recent structure of γTuRC bound to a putative γTuNA dimer (Wieczorek et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 3) and a citation to prior published work (Wieczorek et al., 2020a).

claim: γTuNA dimers directly activate γTuRC-dependent MT nucleation in extract and in vitro.
source: We found that γTuNA dimers directly activate γTuRC-dependent MT nucleation in extract and in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 1, Figure 4, Figure 5) showing γTuNA activation of MT nucleation in extract and in vitro.

claim: γTuNA dimers overcome barriers to MT nucleation posed by the tubulin sequestrator stathmin by enhancing γTuRC's activity at low tubulin concentrations.
source: Finally, we uncovered that γTuNA dimers overcome barriers to MT nucleation posed by the tubulin sequestrator stathmin by enhancing γTuRC's activity at low tubulin concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 6) showing γTuNA activation of MT nucleation in the presence of stathmin.

claim: γTuNA domains are found in myomegalin and the branching factor TPX2.
source: Because γTuNA domains are also found in myomegalin and the branching factor TPX2, among others, our findings are broadly applicable to multiple MTOCs and model eukaryotes from yeast to humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and prior citations in the manuscript (Roubin et al., 2013; Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; King and Petry, 2020b).

claim: Previous work has characterized the structures of γTuNA bound to human and Xenopus γTuRC and observed no obvious structural change.
source: Because previous work has characterized the structures of γTuNA bound to human and Xenopus γTuRC and observed no obvious structural change (Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b), it is possible that binding a γTuNA dimer only transiently biases γTuRC toward the closed ring conformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b).

claim: It is possible that binding a γTuNA dimer only transiently biases γTuRC toward the closed ring conformation.
source: Because previous work has characterized the structures of γTuNA bound to human and Xenopus γTuRC and observed no obvious structural change (Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a; Wieczorek et al., 2020b), it is possible that binding a γTuNA dimer only transiently biases γTuRC toward the closed ring conformation.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from prior structural studies and current experimental data.

claim: Prior modeling suggested that the free energy provided by stochastic binding and lateral association of the first 3–4 tubulin dimers is sufficient to overcome the energy barrier between γTuRC's open and closed states.
source: Furthermore, our own prior modeling suggested that the free energy provided by stochastic binding and lateral association of the first 3–4 tubulin dimers is sufficient to overcome the energy barrier between γTuRC's open and closed states (Thawani et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work by the authors (Thawani et al., 2020).

claim: The γTuNA domain possibly lowers the energy barrier for ring closure.
source: The γTuNA domain possibly lowers this energy barrier for ring closure, as evidenced by its ability to lower γTuRC's critical tubulin concentration.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data showing γTuNA lowers γTuRC's critical tubulin concentration.

claim: Detection of an activated state of vertebrate γTuRC may require the presence of tubulin, GTP, and the γTuNA domain combined with sophisticated structural methods.
source: Ultimately, detection of an activated state of vertebrate γTuRC may require the presence of tubulin, GTP, and the γTuNA domain combined with sophisticated structural methods.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from current experimental data and prior structural studies.

claim: Recent work in yeast suggests that near-closure, or biasing, of the γTuRC ring might require simultaneous binding by multiple CM1/γTuNA domains present in proteins like Spc110p.
source: Intriguingly, recent work in yeast suggests that near-closure, or biasing, of the γTuRC ring might require simultaneous binding by multiple CM1/γTuNA domains present in proteins like Spc110p (Brilot et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Brilot et al., 2021).

claim: Yeast γTuRC appears to have six well-defined CM1/γTuNA binding sites, where overhanging CM1 domains facilitate the formation of the ring by reinforcing lateral interactions between its constituent γ-tubulin small complex (γTuSC) subunits.
source: Unlike in vertebrate structures of γTuRC, yeast γTuRC appears to have six well-defined CM1/γTuNA binding sites, where overhanging CM1 domains facilitate the formation of the ring by reinforcing lateral interactions between its constituent γ-tubulin small complex (γTuSC) subunits (Brilot et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Brilot et al., 2021).

claim: Additional γTuNA binding sites may be present in vertebrate γTuRCs, and simultaneous binding of multiple γTuNAs could further enhance γTuRC activity.
source: This might suggest that additional γTuNA binding sites may also be present in vertebrate γTuRCs, and simultaneous binding of multiple γTuNAs could further enhance γTuRC activity.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from yeast γTuRC structures.

claim: As of yet, any additional γTuNA binding sites have not been detected in vertebrate γTuRC structures.
source: As of yet, any additional γTuNA binding sites have not been detected in vertebrate γTuRC structures, but this possibility is exciting and can actively be investigated with single molecule imaging of fluorescently labeled γTuRC and γTuNA.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: The current model for γTuNA activation of γTuRC involves a direct binding event between a dimerized γTuNA-containing protein (e.g. Cdk5rap2) and γTuRC, which activates γTuRC's MT nucleation ability ~20-fold.
source: Altogether, our current model for γTuNA activation of γTuRC involves a direct binding event between a dimerized γTuNA-containing protein (e.g. Cdk5rap2) and γTuRC, which activates γTuRC's MT nucleation ability ~20-fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 5) showing ~20-fold increase in γTuRC nucleation rate with γTuNA.

claim: This activation overcomes negative regulation by stathmin in the cytoplasm or low local tubulin concentrations.
source: This activation overcomes negative regulation by stathmin in the cytoplasm or low local tubulin concentrations (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 6) showing γTuNA activation of MT nucleation in the presence of stathmin.

claim: Once bound, these activated γTuRCs are enriched by specific MTOCs, like the centrosome, via additional localization motifs present in the γTuNA-containing protein.
source: Once bound, these activated γTuRCs are enriched by specific MTOCs, like the centrosome, via additional localization motifs present in the γTuNA-containing protein.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and prior citations in the manuscript about Cdk5rap2 localization.

claim: Some level of activation may occur outside MTOCs, although recent work hints at how both access to the γTuNA domain and Cdk5rap2 localization is regulated via phosphorylation to prevent ectopic activation.
source: As Cdk5rap2 is also present in the cytoplasm it may be possible that some level of activation also occurs outside MTOCs, although recent work hints at how both access to the γTuNA domain and Cdk5rap2 localization is regulated via phosphorylation to prevent ectopic activation (Conduit et al., 2010; Conduit et al., 2014; Hanafusa et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2017; Tovey et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on citations to prior published work (Conduit et al., 2010; Conduit et al., 2014; Hanafusa et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2017; Tovey et al., 2021).

claim: An estimated 33% of purified γTuRCs likely retain a γTuNA dimer at the end of the purification.
source: Based on our analysis, an estimated 33% of our purified γTuRCs likely retain a γTuNA dimer at the end of the purification (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, which displays Western blot-based determination of γTuNA concentration remaining in γTuRC peak fraction.

claim: The baseline ('buffer') level of γTuRC activity is likely higher than might otherwise be observed with a γTuNA-independent purification.
source: This means that our baseline ('buffer') level of γTuRC activity is likely higher than might otherwise be observed with a γTuNA-independent purification.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that 33% of purified γTuRCs retain γTuNA dimer.

claim: γTuNA dimers might have an even more potent effect on γTuRC activity than reported in this study.
source: We do not believe this slightly elevated baseline level interferes with demonstrating that γTuNA dimers activate γTuRC, but rather stress that γTuNA dimers might have an even more potent effect on γTuRC activity than we report here.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the observation that 33% of purified γTuRCs retain γTuNA dimer.

claim: The region of the γTuNA coil from position 75 to position 77 (F75, L77) is the core γTuNA-γTuRC binding interface.
source: This suggests that the region of the γTuNA coil from position 75 to position 77 (F75, L77) is the core γTuNA-γTuRC binding interface, within which mutations are not well-tolerated for stable γTuRC interaction in extract.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing divergent behavior of mutants at different positions.

claim: Mutations at positions moving from the core towards the N-terminus (L70 to I67 to F63) had less and less impact on both dimerization and γTuRC binding ability in extract.
source: We observed that mutations at positions moving from this core towards the N-terminus (L70 to I67 to F63) had less and less impact on both dimerization and γTuRC binding ability in extract (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3, which displays SEC traces and Western blots showing gradual decrease in impact on dimerization and binding with mutations moving towards N-terminus.

claim: The divergent behavior for L70A and L77A appears to be a result of L70's position outside the most critical region, retaining a small amount of γTuRC binding.
source: Thus, the divergent behavior for L70A and L77A appears to be a result of L70's position outside the most critical region, retaining a small amount of γTuRC binding.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing divergent behavior of L70A and L77A mutants.

claim: The small amount of binding by L70A is not sufficient to significantly activate γTuRC in extract.
source: However, as our extract assays demonstrate in Figure 4, this small amount of binding by L70A is not sufficient to significantly activate γTuRC in extract.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, which displays TIRF microscopy images and quantification showing no significant activation by L70A mutant.

claim: The double I67A/L70A mutant had a strong loss of dimerization but still retained some γTuRC binding, just below the level of the L70A single point mutant.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the double I67A/L70A mutant had a strong loss of dimerization but still retained some γTuRC binding, just below the level of the L70A single point mutant (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and G, which displays Western blots showing residual γTuRC binding for I67A/L70A mutant.

claim: Double substitution to aspartate, instead of alanine, completely removed residual γTuRC binding.
source: By comparing this to the human I67D/L70D mutant (Figure 3F) we found that double substitution to aspartate, instead of alanine, completely removed this residual γTuRC binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F, which displays Western blots showing no γTuRC binding for I67D/L70D mutant.

claim: Retaining some hydrophobicity at positions I67 and L70 might preserve enough of the coil structure to allow for a weak interaction with γTuRC, despite lacking the required hydrophobicity to form a stable coiled-coil dimer.
source: This suggests that retaining some hydrophobicity at these positions might preserve enough of the coil structure to allow for a weak interaction with γTuRC, despite lacking the required hydrophobicity to form a stable coiled-coil dimer (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing divergent behavior of alanine versus aspartate substitutions.

claim: Human I67D/L70D is eluted ahead of human I67A/L70A (~15.0 vs~15.2 mL), indicating that I67D/L70D has a larger hydrodynamic radius despite differing in only two residues.
source: In support of this, closer inspection of the peak SEC retention volumes (Figure 3B–C) reveals that human I67D/L70D is eluted ahead of human I67A/L70A (~15.0 vs~15.2 mL), indicating that I67D/L70D has a larger hydrodynamic radius despite differing in only two residues.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C, which displays SEC traces showing different retention volumes for I67D/L70D and I67A/L70A mutants.

claim: The difference in hydrodynamic radius is reflective of changes in the γTuNA coil structure, where the hydrophilic aspartate residues cause the coil to extend, kink, or otherwise deform in a way that increases the hydrodynamic radius.
source: We believe this difference is reflective of changes in the γTuNA coil structure, where the hydrophilic aspartate residues now cause the coil to extend, kink, or otherwise deform in a way that increases the hydrodynamic radius of the I67D/L70D protein.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3B-C) showing different retention volumes for I67D/L70D and I67A/L70A mutants.

claim: This drastic change in the local coil structure, in addition to blocking coiled-coil dimerization, also likely prevents even weak interactions with γTuRC.
source: This drastic change in the local coil structure, in addition to blocking coiled-coil dimerization, also likely prevents even weak interactions with γTuRC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing no γTuRC binding for I67D/L70D mutant.

claim: Two separate monomeric coils of mutant γTuNA might bind the same γTuRC and form a weak complex.
source: It is possible that two separate monomeric coils of mutant γTuNA might bind the same γTuRC and form a weak complex.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data showing residual binding for I67A/L70A mutant.

claim: In this scenario, the interaction with the γTuRC would stabilize the γTuNA dimer, overcoming the loss of the strongly hydrophobic contacts normally present in the coiled-coil dimer interface.
source: In this scenario, the interaction with the γTuRC would stabilize the γTuNA dimer, overcoming the loss of the strongly hydrophobic contacts normally present in the coiled-coil dimer interface.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data showing residual binding for I67A/L70A mutant.

claim: The late effect of L77A in vitro is reflecting mutant L77A monomers that are stochastically stabilized into a dimer on γTuRC.
source: We hypothesize that this late effect is reflecting mutant L77A monomers that are stochastically stabilized into a dimer on γTuRC (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data (Figure 5) showing late activation by L77A mutant in vitro.

claim: The late effect of L77A is a function of the in vitro environment, which is more permissive of these types of interactions, as L77A does not display this behavior in extract.
source: We further predict that this is also a function of the in vitro environment, which is more permissive of these types of interactions, as L77A does not display this behavior in extract.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data (Figure 4 and Figure 5) showing divergent behavior of L77A mutant in extract versus in vitro.

claim: The fact that I67A/L70A can weakly bind in extract is likely due to the fact that I67 and L70 are outside the critical core region (aa 75–77).
source: The fact that I67A/L70A can weakly bind in extract is likely due to the fact that I67 and L70 are outside the critical core region discussed above (aa 75–77).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing residual binding for I67A/L70A mutant.

claim: Weak binding can only occur in hydrophobic-to-weaker-hydrophobic substituted versions of γTuNA, like I67A/L70A or L77A.
source: Furthermore, we predict that this weak binding can only occur in hydrophobic-to-weaker-hydrophobic substituted versions of γTuNA, like I67A/L70A or L77A.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing divergent behavior of alanine versus aspartate substitutions.

claim: These types of substitutions are not as likely to cause drastic changes to the overall coil structure of a γTuNA monomer, which might allow for two of these monomers to be stabilized into a dimer on γTuRC.
source: These types of substitutions are not as likely to cause drastic changes to the overall coil structure of a γTuNA monomer, which might allow for two of these monomers to be stabilized into a dimer on γTuRC.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing divergent behavior of alanine versus aspartate substitutions.

claim: The γTuNA-GCN4 fusion constructs did not rescue γTuRC binding despite rescuing dimerization.
source: While this did rescue dimerization in an SEC assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), these fusion constructs did not rescue γTuRC binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, which displays SEC traces and Western blots showing no rescue of γTuRC binding with GCN4 fusion.

claim: The fused GCN4 domain did not restore the local coil structure of γTuNA (if impacted).
source: This divergent result is likely because the fused GCN4 domain did not restore the local coil structure of γTuNA (if impacted).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing no rescue of γTuRC binding with GCN4 fusion.

claim: The GCN4 fusion has no impact on the hydrophobic character of the core region (aa 75–77) which appears to be most critical for γTuRC binding in extract.
source: Our GCN4 fusion also has no impact on the hydrophobic character of the core region (aa 75–77) an aspect which appears to be most critical for γTuRC binding in extract.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing importance of core region for γTuRC binding.

claim: Specific residues might be required for both dimerization and for making specific contacts with γTuRC.
source: Also, we suggest that specific residues might be required for both dimerization and for making specific contacts with γTuRC.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing requirement of specific residues for both dimerization and binding.

claim: For cases where specific residues are required for both dimerization and γTuRC binding, inducing dimerization would never be sufficient to restore wildtype levels of γTuRC binding as the specific residue enabling stable interaction would still be missing.
source: For these cases, inducing dimerization would never be sufficient to restore wildtype levels of γTuRC binding as the specific residue enabling stable interaction would still be missing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing no rescue of γTuRC binding with GCN4 fusion.

claim: The core residues, like L77, have twin impacts on both dimerization and stable γTuRC binding.
source: We imagine that the core residues, like L77, have twin impacts on both dimerization and stable γTuRC binding.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing L77's importance for both dimerization and binding.

claim: Dimerization is a key component of how γTuNA interacts with γTuRC.
source: We propose that dimerization is a key component of how γTuNA interacts with γTuRC (supported by the cryo-EM structure by Wieczorek et al., Cell Reports, 2020), but dimerization on its own is not sufficient.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 3) and a citation to prior published work (Wieczorek et al., 2020a).

claim: Dimerization on its own is not sufficient for γTuRC binding and activation.
source: We propose that dimerization is a key component of how γTuNA interacts with γTuRC (supported by the cryo-EM structure by Wieczorek et al., Cell Reports, 2020), but dimerization on its own is not sufficient.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing that GCN4 fusion does not rescue binding.

claim: The F75 residue was required for activation and strong binding in all assays.
source: Indeed, the F75 residue, which would be located on the outer surface of the dimer (Figure 3A), was required for activation and strong binding in all our assays.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 1, Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 5) showing F75A mutant has no binding or activation.

claim: The F75 residue likely has a stabilizing or docking role where this outer surface residue helps 'lock' the γTuNA domain into γTuRC.
source: We hypothesize that this is likely due to a stabilizing or docking role where this outer surface residue helps 'lock' the γTuNA domain into γTuRC.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data (Figure 3) showing F75's importance for binding despite not affecting dimerization.

claim: Liu and colleagues concluded that the N-terminal region of Cdk5rap2 (or CEP215) containing the γTuNA domain had little to no effect on γTuRC MT nucleation in vitro.
source: In their recent structural study of antibody-purified Xenopus γTuRC, Liu and colleagues concluded that the N-terminal region of Cdk5rap2 (or CEP215) containing the γTuNA domain had little to no effect on γTuRC MT nucleation in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 9b from Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Liu et al., 2020).

claim: Liu and colleagues reported that wildtype γTuNA (CEP215N) co-precipitated γ-tubulin, while the F75A mutant did not.
source: They did, however, report that wildtype γTuNA (CEP215N) co-precipitated γ-tubulin, while the F75A mutant did not (Extended Data Fig. 9c from Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Liu et al., 2020).

claim: Liu and colleagues used N-terminally GST tagged versions of γTuNA (CEP215N).
source: Liu and colleagues used N-terminally GST tagged versions of γTuNA (CEP215N).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from prior published work (Liu et al., 2020).

claim: The presence of a large N-terminal tag does not interfere with γTuNA's ability to bind γTuRC.
source: Like our colleagues, we find that the presence of a large N-terminal tag does not interfere with γTuNA's ability to bind γTuRC (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3, which displays Western blots showing γTuRC binding by N-terminally tagged γTuNA.

claim: A bulky N-terminal Halo-tag on γTuNA turns this activator into a specific inhibitor of γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation in extract and in vitro.
source: However, our studies revealed that a bulky N-terminal Halo-tag on γTuNA turns this activator into a specific inhibitor of γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation in extract and in vitro (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, which displays TIRF images showing inhibition of MT nucleation with N-terminally Halo-tagged γTuNA.

claim: The inhibitory effect of N-terminal Halo-tag is likely due to the steric clash produced by two copies of the bulky N-terminal tag in proximity to the critical nucleation interface on the γ-tubulin ring.
source: This is likely due to the steric clash produced by two copies of the bulky N-terminal tag in proximity to the critical nucleation interface on the γ-tubulin ring.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) showing inhibition with N-terminally Halo-tagged γTuNA.

claim: Differences in the distance between the bulky tag and γTuNA, as well as the ratio of γTuNA to γTuRC tested, determines whether an activation effect is possible.
source: This suggests that differences in the distance between the bulky tag and γTuNA, as well as the ratio of γTuNA to γTuRC tested, determines whether an activation effect is possible.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and comparison to prior published work (Muroyama et al., 2016).

claim: If multiple γTuNA binding sites exist in vertebrate γTuRCs (as in yeast), then the N-terminal tag effect might be further compounded as multiple steric clashes could be present.
source: If it is true that multiple γTuNA binding sites exist in vertebrate γTuRCs (as in yeast; Brilot et al., 2021), then this N-terminal tag effect might be further compounded as multiple steric clashes could be present.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data and citation to prior published work (Brilot et al., 2021).

claim: The original reports from the Qi group used the small FLAG tag.
source: We note that the original reports from the Qi group used the small FLAG tag (Choi et al., 2010), and our work is based on the small Strep-His tag at the N-terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Choi et al., 2010).

claim: N-terminally 6xHis-tagged γTuNA activates MT nucleation in extract.
source: Although N-terminally 6xHis-tagged γTuNA activates MT nucleation in extract (as presented in Figure 1 of this study), it had little to no effect on the original antibody-purified Xenopus γTuRC in vitro (Figure 6 in Thawani et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study (Figure 1).

claim: N-terminally 6xHis-tagged γTuNA had little to no effect on the original antibody-purified Xenopus γTuRC in vitro.
source: Although N-terminally 6xHis-tagged γTuNA activates MT nucleation in extract (as presented in Figure 1 of this study), it had little to no effect on the original antibody-purified Xenopus γTuRC in vitro (Figure 6 in Thawani et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work by the authors (Thawani et al., 2020).

claim: The Halo-γTuNA purification method is routinely at least 20-fold higher yield, higher purity, and ultimately has more robust activity than the antibody-based method.
source: Since then, we developed the Halo-γTuNA purification method described here, which is routinely at least 20-fold higher yield, higher purity, and ultimately has more robust activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study comparing the new Halo-γTuNA purification method to the previous antibody-based method.

claim: The increased density of nucleation competent γTuRCs present in the single molecule assays resulted in better detection of γTuNA's activation effect.
source: This resulted in increased density of nucleation competent γTuRCs present in our single molecule assays, as well as better detection of γTuNA's activation effect.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing improved γTuRC purification and detection of γTuNA activation effect.

claim: Silver staining the peak γTuRC fraction for the new prep showed the same banding pattern as that published with the previous antibody prepped γTuRC, indicating that aside from γTuRC components, there was no obvious major factor present to explain the response to γTuNA.
source: Silver staining the peak γTuRC fraction for our new prep (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) showed the same banding pattern as that published with our previous antibody prepped γTuRC, indicating that aside from γTuRC components, there was no obvious major factor present to explain the response to γTuNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, which displays silver stain of peak γTuRC fraction.

claim: The difference in γTuNA activation effect can be explained by the greater yield and consistent quality of γTuRC provided by the Halo-γTuNA prep.
source: Rather, we believe the difference can be explained by the greater yield and consistent quality of γTuRC provided by the Halo-γTuNA prep.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing the new Halo-γTuNA purification method to the previous antibody-based method.

claim: This study validates and extends the original γTuNA studies by the Qi group.
source: As such, we validate and extend the original γTuNA studies by the Qi group.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and citations to prior published work by the Qi group (Fong et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010).

claim: The nucleoside diphosphate kinase 7 (NME7) was detected in the mass spectrometry analysis.
source: We also detected the nucleoside diphosphate kinase 7 (better known as NME7).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from the current study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: NME7 is a γTuRC subunit that is present regardless of how γTuRC is purified or whether γTuNA is present.
source: This agrees with prior work showing that NME7 is a γTuRC subunit that is present regardless of how γTuRC is purified or whether γTuNA is present (Hutchins et al., Science, 2010; Teixido-Traversa et al., Mol Biol Cell, 2010; Liu et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020; Consolati et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Hutchins et al., 2010; Teixido-Traversa et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020; Consolati et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020a).

claim: Three unique proteins were detected that were enriched at a higher level than NME7 and had not been reported to directly interact with γTuRC or γTuNA.
source: Surprisingly, we detected three unique proteins that were enriched at a higher level than NME7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and had not been reported to directly interact with γTuRC or γTuNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The three unique proteins detected were the cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) subunits A and B, as well as the type II delta chain of the calmodulin-dependent protein kinase (CAMK2D).
source: These were the cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) subunits A and B, as well as the type II delta chain of the calmodulin-dependent protein kinase (CAMK2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from the current study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: CDK1 subunits A and B, and CAMK2D might be novel co-factors for γTuRC.
source: Hence, these might be novel co-factors for γTuRC.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from mass spectrometry data showing enrichment of these proteins.
